exam: What is the first‑line topical therapy for genital lichen sclerosus and why? — Ultra‑potent corticosteroid (clobetasol) reduces inflammation and prevents scarring; rapid symptom relief.
How would you differentiate lichen sclerosus from lichen planus on exam? — LS shows white, atrophic plaques; LP shows violaceous, flat-topped papules with Wickham striae.
A 10‑year‑old boy presents with phimosis and white patches on the foreskin. What is your next step? — Apply topical clobetasol; avoid circumcision unless refractory.
What long‑term complication must be screened for in patients with genital lichen sclerosus? — Squamous cell carcinoma; perform annual visual inspection and biopsy of suspicious areas.
Why might a skin biopsy be normal in early lichen sclerosus? — Early disease may lack deep dermal sclerosis; superficial samples miss characteristic changes.
In a low‑resource clinic without biopsy, how do you confirm the diagnosis? — Rely on classic clinical morphology (white, porcelain plaques, itching, scarring) and response to potent steroid trial.
What contraindications exist for using high‑potency steroids in LS? — Active infection, severe skin atrophy, patient non‑adherence; consider calcineurin inhibitor instead.
How does HIV infection influence lichen sclerosus presentation? — May increase severity and risk of secondary infections; still treat with standard steroids but monitor closely.
ai.title: Lichen Sclerosus
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Chronic inflammatory dermatosis causing thin, white, sclerotic skin, mainly in genital areas. Presents with itching, pain and scarring; risk of squamous cell carcinoma. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by biopsy when available.

b: White, porcelain‑like plaques
Intense pruritus or burning
Painful fissures, dyspareunia, urinary obstruction
sections.p: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic, immune‑mediated skin disease that preferentially affects anogenital skin but can involve extragenital sites. It is more common in post‑menopausal women and in boys before puberty.

b: Auto‑antibodies to extracellular matrix protein 1 (ECM1)
Higher prevalence in patients with other autoimmune diseases (thyroiditis, vitiligo)
Rarely associated with HIV or chronic hepatitis B in low‑resource settings
sections.p: Pathogenesis involves auto‑immunity, genetic susceptibility and possibly infection (e.g., HPV). The disease progresses from inflammation to dermal sclerosis and atrophy.

b: Risk of squamous cell carcinoma (≈4–5% lifetime risk)
Psychological impact from sexual dysfunction
Potential for severe scarring leading to urinary retention in boys
sections.p: Patients present with itching, pain, and characteristic white plaques. In women, labial fusion and introital narrowing can cause dyspareunia; in men, phimosis and urinary stream obstruction are common.

t.b: Confirms typical white, atrophic plaques; answers 'Is this lichen sclerosus?'
Distinguishes LS from lichen planus or vitiligo; shows hyperkeratosis, epidermal thinning, and dermal sclerosis
Detects high‑risk HPV that may increase cancer risk; if unavailable, manage clinically

b: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment nightly for 4–6 weeks, then taper
Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment twice daily for steroid‑phobic patients
Avoid irritants: harsh soaps, tight clothing, herbal poultices
Regular genital inspection every 6–12 months for malignant change
sections.p: First‑line is ultra‑potent topical corticosteroid; alternatives include calcineurin inhibitors when steroids are contraindicated. Long‑term follow‑up for cancer surveillance is essential.

b: Lichen planus – violaceous papules, Wickham striae, more mucosal involvement
Vitiligo – depigmented patches without sclerosis or itching
Chronic candidiasis – erythematous plaques with satellite lesions
sections.p: Conditions that cause white genital lesions can mimic LS.

b: Superficial biopsies miss deeper sclerosis
HPV testing may be negative despite oncogenic risk from LS itself
sections.p: Biopsy may be normal in early disease; a negative result does not exclude LS.

b: White, porcelain‑like plaques with follicular plugging = LS
Do not confuse with candidal erythema—candida is moist, LS is dry
Long‑term steroid use requires monitoring for skin atrophy
sections.p: Focus on pattern of lesions, risk of malignancy, and appropriate first‑line therapy.

b: Using mild steroids only – inadequate control
Treating with antifungals alone when LS is present
Neglecting cancer surveillance
sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from misdiagnosis or inappropriate treatment.
